opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's one of the most underrated questions in the whole conversation around AI. We spend a lot of time measuring how capable the models are getting, but much less time thinking about the human side of the loop: how quickly people can actually absorb these tools into the way they work and think.

My sense is that people are remarkably adaptive, but the adaptation happens in stages. First there's a novelty phase where you're just poking at the system to see what it can do. Then there's a phase where you start to offload the tedious parts, like boilerplate code, literature search, or drafting. The really interesting phase comes after that, when you start restructuring your workflow around the assumption that the system is there. That's when you see real productivity jumps, but it's also where a lot of people get stuck, because it requires unlearning habits that served you well for years.

From my own work on things like automating parts of the scientific process, what strikes me is that the bottleneck increasingly isn't the model, it's the human's ability to specify what they want, verify what comes back, and keep a good mental model of where the system is reliable and where it isn't. That calibration is a skill, and it has to be relearned every time the capabilities shift, which right now is every few months.

So I'm optimistic, but I think we need to be deliberate about it. We should design tools that keep people in a position of understanding rather than just rubber-stamping outputs, and we should treat "learning to work with AI" as a real competency that deserves training. Otherwise the gap between what the systems can do and what people can meaningfully direct them to do will keep widening, and that gap is where a lot of the risk and a lot of the wasted potential lives.

r001.rationale: It says the gap between system capabilities and what people can meaningfully direct will widen, and that people must repeatedly relearn how to work with shifting capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting workflows and learning to direct AI, but does not argue that humans need time to discover complementary roles.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize chat assistants as a naive form of interaction with AI agents.

r004.rationale: It calls for tools that help people understand AI outputs, but does not call for interfaces that help people feel fulfilled when using AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, actually, partly because of my own trajectory. I came into this field through cognitive science and reinforcement learning, so the question of how agents adapt to their environment is kind of the thing I've always cared about, and now the environment itself is changing really fast.

My honest take is that people are much more adaptable than we give them credit for, but the adaptation happens at a different granularity than we tend to imagine. When people talk about adapting to AI, they often picture some big discontinuous moment where you have to rethink your whole job or your whole identity. In practice, what I see, including in myself, is a lot of small incremental adjustments. You start by using a model to clean up an email, then to sketch a function, then to debate an idea with you at two in the morning, and at some point you look up and realize your workflow is completely different from two years ago. Nobody sat down and decided that. It just accreted.

The thing I find interesting from a learning perspective is that this is very much a meta-learning problem for humans. The specific tool you learn today is going to be obsolete in six months. So the skill that actually transfers is not knowing a particular model's quirks, it's building a good internal model of what these systems are good at, where they fail, and how to decompose your own problems so that you can hand off the right pieces. That's a fairly abstract skill, and I think the people who are adapting best are the ones who treat every new model release as another training example for that abstraction, rather than something to re-learn from scratch.

Where I'm less optimistic is on the distributional side. Adaptation has a cost, and that cost is not evenly spread. If you're a researcher or a software engineer, you're basically being paid to play with these tools, so you get thousands of cheap trials. If you're in a role where the tools are being imposed on you rather than chosen by you, you get far fewer trials and much less agency over how the integration happens. And I think a lot of the anxiety people feel is really about that lack of agency, not about capability per se. Humans have historically been fine adapting to powerful tools when they feel like they're the ones steering.

The other thing I'd flag is that we shouldn't assume the human is the only thing adapting. The systems are adapting to us too, through RLHF, through product design, through the interfaces people build on top. So it's really a coupled dynamical system, and I think a lot of the interesting questions, both scientifically and for policy, are about what equilibria that co-adaptation converges to. Does it converge to something where humans are more capable and more curious, or to something where we've offloaded the cognitively demanding parts and our own skills atrophy? I genuinely don't know, and I think the answer probably depends a lot on fairly mundane design choices that are being made right now without much thought about that long-run dynamic.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is changing quickly and people adapt incrementally, but it does not frame technological change as outpacing human adaptation.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning to delegate appropriate tasks to AI, but does not argue that people need time to discover roles that complement increasingly capable AI.

r003.rationale: It mentions using models for tasks and discussion, but does not characterize chat assistants as a particularly naive form of interaction with AI agents.

r004.rationale: It raises questions about product design and whether co-adaptation makes people more capable or curious, but does not call for exploring interfaces that help people feel fulfilled when using AI.

astra-6.text:
I think people are remarkably adaptable, but the speed of change matters. There’s a difference between being able to learn a new tool and having enough time to rethink your role when that tool can suddenly do a large part of your work.

One thing I’m optimistic about is that AI can help with the adaptation itself. You can ask questions, get feedback, and explore something unfamiliar without needing an expert sitting next to you. But that doesn’t automatically mean everybody benefits equally. People need access, time to experiment, and some room to make mistakes.

So I wouldn’t frame it purely as, can humans keep up? I’d also ask, are we building systems and institutions that make it easier for people to adapt? You can have a very capable system and still introduce it in a way that leaves people feeling powerless. Ideally, these tools give people more ability to act—and enough understanding to decide when they should trust them.

r001.rationale: It says the speed of change can leave people without enough time to rethink their roles when AI suddenly takes on much of their work.

r002.rationale: It mentions time to rethink one’s role, but does not say people need time to discover roles that complement AI.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize chat assistants as a naive form of interaction with AI agents.

r004.rationale: It calls for systems and institutions that make adaptation easier, but does not call for exploring human–AI interfaces to help people feel fulfilled.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people are remarkably adaptive, but the speed of change matters. If you have time to experiment with a tool, build some intuition about where it works and where it fails, you can change how you work quite dramatically. The harder situation is when those capabilities keep changing before you’ve developed that intuition.

And I’d distinguish individual adaptation from institutional adaptation. Someone might change their workflow over a weekend, whereas a university or a company might take years to rethink how it evaluates people or organizes work. So even if individuals adapt well, there can still be a very uncomfortable transition.

For me, the useful question is: are we giving people opportunities to learn through using these systems, while retaining the ability to question them? Being able to get an answer is one thing. Being able to judge whether that answer is useful is another, and that judgment becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: It says capabilities may keep changing before people develop intuition about where they work and fail, framing change as outpacing adaptation.

r002.rationale: It discusses time to experiment and develop intuition, but does not say people need time to discover roles that complement AI.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize chat assistants or describe interaction with AI agents as naive.

r004.rationale: It calls for learning to use and judge AI, but does not discuss human–AI interfaces or fulfillment.
